title: Secure Devices & Safe Browsing
summary: Updates, downloads, Wi-Fi and the everyday habits that keep devices clean.

lessons.title: Update everything
points: Updates fix security holes that attackers actively exploit. Turn on automatic updates for your operating system, browser and apps.
Restart when prompted. Many updates only take effect after a restart.
Devices that no longer receive security updates (end-of-life) should be replaced.

lessons.title: Download carefully
points: Install software only from official app stores or the vendor's own website, and at work only from approved sources.
Be wary of 'cracked' software, browser extensions with excessive permissions and fake 'update your player' pop-ups.
Sponsored search results can be malicious ads. Check the domain before downloading.

lessons.title: Wi-Fi and travel
points: Public Wi-Fi can be fake or monitored. Prefer your phone's hotspot or your organisation's VPN for work.
Check you're on HTTPS for anything sensitive, and turn off auto-join for open networks.
Use a privacy screen and keep devices with you when travelling.

lessons.title: Lost device? Act fast
points: Use a PIN or biometric lock and keep full-disk encryption on (BitLocker, FileVault, or built-in phone encryption).
Report a lost or stolen device immediately so it can be locked or wiped remotely.
Don't disable security tools such as antivirus or endpoint protection, even if they seem slow.

questions.q: Why are software updates important for security?
options: They only add new emojis
They fix vulnerabilities attackers can exploit
They make devices slower on purpose
They're only needed for games
questions.why: Most updates include security fixes. Delaying them leaves known holes open.

questions.q: A pop-up on a website says your video player is out of date and offers a download. It's safe to install it.
questions.why: Fake update prompts are a common malware delivery trick. Update software only through its own settings or official store.

questions.q: You need to send a work document from a café. What's the safest option?
options: Connect to the open café Wi-Fi
Use your phone hotspot or company VPN
Ask the barista for their laptop
Email it from a personal account
questions.why: Your own hotspot or a VPN avoids untrusted networks. Personal accounts may break data-handling rules.

questions.q: Your work laptop is stolen from your car. What should you do first?
options: Wait to see if it turns up
Report it to IT/security immediately
Buy a new one quietly
Change your desktop wallpaper
questions.why: Fast reporting allows remote lock/wipe and session revocation before data is accessed.

questions.q: Full-disk encryption helps protect data if a device is lost or stolen.
questions.why: Without the key, an encrypted drive's data is unreadable, even if the drive is removed.

questions.q: A browser extension that changes page colours asks to 'read and change all your data on all websites'. What should you do?
options: Accept, all extensions ask this
Decline, the permission is far more than it needs
Install it on a work device only
Accept and uninstall later
questions.why: Over-privileged extensions can read passwords and session data. Choose tools whose permissions match their purpose.

questions.q: It's fine to turn off endpoint protection if it slows down your computer.
questions.why: Security tools protect you and your organisation. Report performance problems to IT instead of disabling protection.

questions.q: Which source is safest for downloading software at work?
options: A top search ad
A file-sharing forum
Your organisation's approved software portal
A link in a chat from a stranger
questions.why: Approved portals deliver vetted, licensed software. Search ads and forums are common malware sources.

questions.q: An old laptop that no longer gets security updates is safe as long as it has antivirus.
questions.why: End-of-life systems accumulate unpatched vulnerabilities that antivirus can't fully cover. Replace or isolate them.

questions.q: What's a good habit for phones and laptops?
options: No screen lock so it's faster
A PIN or biometric lock with auto-lock enabled
Share your PIN with your team
Use 0000 as a PIN
questions.why: A screen lock with a short auto-lock time is the simplest protection against casual access.
